title: What Is in the Box: A Release Bundle With a Manifest That Checks Itself, and the Four Ways Files Differ From It

questions.question: A download stops half way. What in the manifest finds it?
options: The file sizes, which add up short
The end line, which holds the hash of everything above it: its absence is no end line, and a changed manifest is bad checksum
The version line, which is missing
The sorted order, which is broken
questions.explanation: A manifest cut short has no end line, and one that was changed no longer matches the hash in its end line. Each gets its own reason.

questions.question: Why is the manifest sorted by path?
options: Sorting makes the parser faster
So that the files are unpacked in order
Because paths are compared as text
The same release in any order gives the same text, so the manifest can itself be compared and hashed
questions.explanation: If the text depended on the order the files were listed in, the same release would have many manifests and none could be compared or hashed.

questions.question: Why does the manifest refuse ../../etc/passwd as a path?
options: It is an absolute path
The updater writes at that path: an archive that escapes the directory overwrites the system unpacking it, and the manifest has to refuse it before any file is written
It has more than one dot
It is longer than a path may be
questions.explanation: An archive that can name a path outside its own directory can overwrite the system that unpacks it. The refusal has to come before anything is written.

questions.question: Which difference can a size check not see?
options: A file that never arrived
A file left over from an older release
A byte changed in place: same size, different hash
A file cut short by a byte
questions.explanation: One byte of bin/robot_node was changed and the size stayed the same. Only the hash of the contents shows it.

questions.question: Why is a stale file from an older release a problem?
options: It is part of what is running, since a program may load it by name, and it is not part of the release
It takes up space on the robot
Its name is not in the right directory
It slows down the verification
questions.explanation: bin/old_tool was left by release 1.3. Something may still load it by name, so the robot is running a file that no release describes.

questions.question: Why is FNV-1a not enough for a real release?
options: It is too slow for large files
Its 64 bits collide too often for 1000 files
Anyone can recompute it: a real release is signed with a key kept at the build machine, which needs a cryptographic library this curriculum does not write
It cannot hash an empty file
questions.explanation: It caught 1000 of 1000 single bit flips, which is accident. Someone who changes a file on purpose can also change the hash, which only a signature prevents.
